label: On the way
rationale: Updates from the journey: I'm at the station, the roads are jammed, a seat's come free, I rode past my stop.
mixUps: Crowded is konderu and a free seat is aiteru, while a whole empty train or road is suiteru, never isogashii or hima. Arriving takes ni (eki ni tsuku), but the stop you ride past takes o (eki o norisugosu).

targets.trap: eki ni touchaku suru is correct but stiff, the language of announcements and work emails; in conversation you arrive with tsuku, and 'I'm here' is the past tsuita.
targets.use: Mostly a phone or text update: ima eki tsuita (I'm at the station now), eki tsuitara renraku suru (I'll text when I get there). The past tsuita is how you say 'I'm here'; casual speech drops ni.
targets.notes: nanji ni tsuku? (what time do you get in?) and mou sugu tsuku (almost there) are the other everyday forms.

example.romaji: eki tsuitara, kaisatsu no mae de matteru ne.
example.ja: 駅着いたら、改札の前で待ってるね。
example.english: When I get to the station, I'll wait in front of the ticket gates.

examplePolite.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, kaisatsu no mae de mattemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅に着いたら、改札の前で待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: When I get to the station, I'll wait in front of the ticket gates.

targets.verbSense: get crowded; konderu = be crowded, packed
targets.trap: Not michi ga isogashii: isogashii is for people and their time (isogashii hi, a busy day), never for a place full of people or cars. A busy road, train or shop is konderu ('has got packed').
targets.use: Heard as konderu (busy now) or kondete (because it was busy), usually without ga: michi konderu kara okureru kamo. Plain komu is for patterns: kono jikan wa michi komu yo (the roads get busy at this hour). Same verb as mise ga komu and densha konderu. (sugoi konderu, with sugoi as an adverb, is casual; sugoku is the standard form.)
targets.notes: A full jam is juutai: juutai ni hamatta (I got stuck in traffic). Clear roads are suiteru: michi suiteta.

example.ja: 今日、道すごい混んでるね。
example.english: The roads are really busy today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa michi ga sugoku kondemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は道がすごく混んでますね。
examplePolite.english: The roads are really busy today.

targets.english: a seat frees up (aiteru = a seat is free)
targets.verbSense: become empty or vacant; open up (a space, a slot)
targets.trap: Not kono seki tada? (that asks if it costs nothing) or seki ga hima: hima is a person or a quiet shop with nothing going on, and a free seat is aiteru ('has come open'). For your own schedule both work: ashita aiteru? / ashita hima?
targets.use: Almost always heard as aiteru: koko aitemasu ka? (is this seat free?) or seki aiteru (there's a free seat). aita is the moment one frees up: a, seki aita.
targets.notes: A whole train being empty or packed is densha ga suiteru / konderu, not aiteru.

example.ja: あ、あそこ席空いてるよ。
example.english: Oh, there's a free seat over there.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、この席空いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, is this seat free?

targets.trap: Not eki o nogasu or eki o misu shita: staying on past your stop is norisugosu (ride past), and nogasu is for a train that left without you. orisokoneta (didn't manage to get off) also works, say on a packed train.
targets.use: Nearly always in the past, norisugoshita or norisugoshichatta, and usually without eki: nechatte norisugoshita (I fell asleep and missed my stop). How far you went is counted in stops: hitoeki norisugoshita. When the noun is said, it's oriru eki: oriru eki norisugoshita (I went past my stop).
targets.notes: Sleeping through the stop is also nesugoshita; oversleeping in the morning is nebou shita.

example.ja: 寝ちゃって、一駅乗り過ごした。
example.english: I fell asleep and went one stop too far.

examplePolite.ja: 寝てしまって、一駅乗り過ごしました。
examplePolite.english: I fell asleep and went one stop too far.
